items.title: Consolidation
items.stakes: Three monitoring systems become one at 02:00 UTC. Fourteen minutes later, 212 rooms are red and none of them is broken.
items.clock: Before Tahvara's town hall at 13:00 local — 05:00 UTC.
items.reward: One operations centre that sees the estate as it is, and a real alarm that reached its owner in time.

objectives.text: Decide what to do with 212 red rooms
Decide what happens to the UPS alarm

items.sub: Saturday · 02:14 UTC · Friday 21:14 Harrowmere · Saturday 10:14 Tahvara

items.alt: The global operations centre at night; the estate map dotted red across Valmera and Tahvara; clocks read 21:14, 03:14 and 10:14. Yuki points at the wall; Maya on the phone with Henrik.

bubbles.text: Two hundred and twelve rooms red. Flapping every two minutes.

items.caption: Fourteen minutes after cutover.

lines.text: Two hundred and twelve. Every two minutes. Dev muted Tahvara.
Unmute it — narrowly. Then we find out why working rooms look dead.

items.prompt: 02:16 UTC. 212 rooms flapping red. What do you do?
items.risk: A real outage hidden in a flood — or silenced with it.
timeout: Dev mutes Tahvara to stop the noise.

hints.text: Are they really down? What else is still watching them?

options.label: Mute all Valmera and Tahvara alarms until morning
options.result: The screen goes quiet — and everything real in two regions goes quiet with it.
options.consequence: Silencing regions to stop one false alarm.

options.label: Hold at the runbook's checkpoint — the old regional systems keep running in parallel — and check five red rooms directly
options.result: All five are working; the old systems show them green.
options.consequence: Stop, compare, look at real rooms.

options.label: Roll the whole migration back now
options.result: Two months of work reversed for a threshold.
options.consequence: The rollback criteria aren't met; the old systems are already there.

options.label: Acknowledge all 212
options.result: An hour of clicking. They're red again in two minutes.

items.title: 212 red, zero broken.
items.body: Valmera's and Tahvara's controllers send a heartbeat every 120 seconds — a recorded regional design for sites on metered links. The new centre's template waits 60 seconds. Every gap between heartbeats looks like a death; every heartbeat, a resurrection. The sites' design files say: allow three missed beats — 360 seconds. The migration plan never read them.
items.label: Test: how often does each device look dead — and what should the timeout be?

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Yuki and Maya beside a board. Two hundred and twelve rooms red, every two minutes. Their heartbeats come every hundred and twenty seconds; the new NOC gives up after sixty. So every gap looks like a death. Their site files say allow three missed beats — three hundred and sixty seconds. And somewhere under two hundred and twelve false alarms is a real one.

items.caption: Advanced: the formula is there if you ask. Try without it first.

items.text: 📙 ON REQUEST · ADVANCED  Terms   Cutover   Parallel run   Alarm flood   UPS runtime   If you need it   ƒ Ask for the formula · Heartbeat timeout   ƒ FORMULA · Heartbeat timeout  T timeout  ≥ k × T interval    T interval   time between a device's heartbeats  k  heartbeats that may be missed before an alarm (often 3)  T timeout   how long the monitor waits before calling the device down      ƒ Ask for the formula · UPS runtime (rough)   ƒ FORMULA · UPS runtime (rough)  t = E batt  × η ÷ P load    E batt   battery energy, Wh  η  inverter efficiency, about 0.9  P load   load on the UPS, W  t  runtime, h

items.label: **Learn it now:** cutovers, thresholds and alarm floods.

Act II — “The alarm under the mute”

items.title: The alarm under the mute.
items.body: At 02:20, before anyone could stop him, the other night analyst right-clicked Tahvara and chose ‘Mute region…’. Narrowing it to heartbeat flaps brings one alarm to the top: Tahvara HQ's auditorium UPS, on battery since 02:20 after a utility fault. Tahvara's regional town hall is in that auditorium at 13:00 local — 05:00 UTC.
items.label: Test: how long is left — and whose decision is it?

items.alt: An operations sheet at 03:25 UTC: 212 rooms red, flapping every 120 s; heartbeat every 120 s against a 60 s timeout; a dark banner ‘MUTED: ALL TAHVARA (02:20)’; under the mute, in red, the HQ auditorium UPS on battery since 02:20, about 43 minutes left, town hall at 05:00 UTC.
items.caption: One real alarm under two hundred and twelve false ones.

items.label: **Triage it:** the first hour after cutover.

items.prompt: 03:27 UTC. The UPS has about 43 minutes at its present load. What do you do?
items.risk: A dark auditorium at the start of the town hall.
timeout: The call waits for the flood to settle.
At 04:08 UTC the auditorium's UPS runs out.

hints.text: Whose UPS — and what number helps them decide?

options.label: Remote into the UPS and change its settings to stretch the battery

Call Tahvara facilities now with the numbers — on battery since 02:20 UTC, about 43 minutes at 1,200 W, about 74 if non-critical loads are shed — and let them decide; warn the town-hall organisers of the risk
options.result: Facilities shed the LED wall and two racks at 03:35; the utility crew restores power at 04:25 UTC. The town hall starts on time.
options.consequence: Their power, your countdown, the organisers told.

options.label: Wait and see if the utility comes back
options.result: At 04:08 UTC the auditorium goes dark.
options.fail: A countdown belongs to someone who can act on it.

options.label: Move the town hall to Valmera
options.result: It's 04:27 there, and a different country.

items.title: A hundred alarms in minutes
items.body: In March 1979, at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, operators faced more than a hundred alarms within the first few minutes of an accident, many sounding at once, with the most important ones hard to pick out. The inquiries that followed made the design of alarms — how many, how shown, which first — a field of engineering in its own right.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #71 · AVERY'S LENS  An alarm must be rare enough to read  When everything is red, nothing is. Thresholds come from each system's design, and silencing is scoped, owned and time-limited — never ‘mute all’.  212 false alarms buried one real one, and the bulk mute that stopped the noise hid a UPS running out on the morning of a town hall.

items.alt: The operations sheet after the fixes: no rooms flapping; site thresholds imported (360 s for the 120 s sites); a green suppression box — heartbeat flaps only, owner Yuki, expires 06:00; UPS load shed to 700 W and utility back at 04:25; the old regional systems running in parallel for 14 days.
items.caption: Every alarm rare enough to read.

items.prompt: Dev only muted it because we couldn't see anything else. Is he in trouble?

options.label: “No. The system made muting everything the easiest button. We'll make the right one easier — scoped, owned, expiring.”
options.reply: I'll tell him. He's been staring at the floor for ten minutes.

options.label: “He should have known better.”
options.reply: At two in the morning with two hundred alarms? Would you?

items.title: timeout: 60 s (global)
items.body: The consolidated centre's device template: ‘heartbeat timeout 60 s · global’. Written for Harrowmere's controllers, which beat every 30 s. Valmera's and Tahvara's design files — 120 s, for metered links — weren't read in the migration plan.

items.prompt: Monday. What are the new centre's rules?
items.risk: The next flood, and the next buried alarm.
timeout: The rules stay as they were.
Next month's firmware alarms flood the same wall.

hints.text: What would have made tonight boring?

options.label: One global template; the regions change their heartbeats to match
options.result: Tahvara's metered links triple in cost.
options.consequence: Erasing a recorded design for the tool's convenience.

options.label: Thresholds come from each site's design file; no bulk mutes — only scoped suppressions with an owner and an expiry; the old systems run in parallel for two weeks with a daily comparison; rollback criteria stay in the runbook
options.result: After fourteen days the two views agree to the room; the old systems retire.
options.consequence: Design carried across; silence narrow and owned; proof before retirement.

options.label: Go back to three regional centres for good
options.result: Three sets of night shifts, three truths.

options.label: Set every timeout to an hour
options.result: No more floods — and no outage seen for an hour.
options.fail: A monitor must still see what matters.

items.sub: Two weeks later · the old systems switched off

items.alt: The operations centre by day; the estate map calm; a sticky note on the old regional server reads RETIRED. Henrik and Maya in front of the wall.

bubbles.text: Forty sites on one wall. And I understand what I'm looking at.
Seventy-eight percent designed, twenty-two drift — now fifteen. And a town hall that never knew.

items.title: Mute region…
items.body: The new centre's console: right-click any region → ‘Mute region…’ — one click, no expiry, no owner. The suppression editor that scopes a single rule is three menus deeper.

items.alt: A call from an old colleague: Odile, the architect from the Playhouse, on the phone in a design studio full of drawings; Maya on the other end.

bubbles.text: The Wyndmere Centre for the Performing Arts. The building tops out next month and their design lead has quit. They asked who wrote Corvane's standard.
A building that isn't finished yet?

items.caption: END OF SEASON 7 · The boss level is next. Then: *Topping Out.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A cutover needs a way back: checkpoints, written rollback criteria, the old system running in parallel. Thresholds carry design — T timeout  ≥ k × T interval  — so import them from the site files. Never mute everything: suppress one false condition, with an owner and an expiry. Give the owner of a countdown the number (t = E × η ÷ P, roughly) and let them decide.
REFLECTION (optional)  · A season of forty sites: which difference you found this year turned out to be somebody’s good decision?
